challenge.e.acl.decision: ACLs are evaluated top to bottom; the first match decides. Here a deny (or the implicit deny at the end) in ACL {{acl}} ({{dir}}) matches.
challenge.e.acl.dir: The ACL is applied on the interface in the “{{dir}}” direction: “in” checks packets as they arrive, “out” as they leave the router.
challenge.e.acl.reply: Cisco routers report packets dropped by an ACL with ICMP destination unreachable, code 13 (communication administratively prohibited) – which is why ping shows “U”.
challenge.e.gen.layer.host: The receiver unwraps the PDU up to the highest layer it contains: layer {{layer}}.
challenge.e.gen.layer.hub: A hub works at layer 1 only: it repeats electrical signals.
challenge.e.gen.layer.router: A router decides by IP address (layer 3); it looks at the transport layer only for ACLs and NAT.
challenge.e.gen.layer.switch: A switch decides based on layer 2 (MAC addresses, VLAN tag). Higher layers are just payload to it.
challenge.e.host.arpBcast: The sender does not know the MAC yet, so the request goes to the broadcast address – everyone in the segment hears it.
challenge.e.host.arpNotMine: Only the owner of the requested address ({{ip}}) answers. Everyone else ignores the request.
challenge.e.host.arpReply: The mapping {{ip}} → {{mac}} goes into the ARP cache; the held-back IP packet is then sent.
challenge.e.host.arpReq: The host owns {{ip}} and answers with a unicast carrying its MAC; it also learns the mapping for {{sender}}.
challenge.e.host.closedPort.tcp: Nobody listens on TCP port {{port}}. The host refuses the connection with an RST.
challenge.e.host.closedPort.udp: Nobody listens on UDP port {{port}}. The host answers with ICMP destination unreachable / port unreachable.
challenge.e.host.echoMatch: Echo request and reply carry the same identifier and sequence number. ICMP has no ports.
challenge.e.host.echoReq: A ping to the host's own address is answered: it sends an echo reply with swapped addresses and the same ID/sequence to {{src}}.
challenge.e.host.nic: The NIC accepts only frames for its own MAC, broadcasts and subscribed multicasts. This frame ({{dst}}) is not for it.
challenge.e.host.notMine: A host is not a router: packets not addressed to it ({{dst}}) are discarded.
challenge.e.hub.action: A hub works at layer 1: it amplifies and repeats the signal out all {{count}} other ports without looking at MAC addresses.
challenge.e.nat.in: The NAT table maps {{global}} (inside global) to the inside host {{local}} (inside local); the reply's destination is translated back.
challenge.e.nat.out: When leaving the inside network, NAT swaps the private source address {{local}} for the inside global address {{global}} (with PAT also the source port).
challenge.e.rt.action.forward: There is a route to {{dst}} (next hop {{via}} via {{port}}), the TTL is greater than 1 and no ACL blocks it – the router forwards.
challenge.e.rt.arp.no: The MAC of {{via}} is already known (ARP cache), so the packet goes out immediately.
challenge.e.rt.arp.yes: The MAC of {{via}} is missing from the ARP cache; the router sends an ARP request first and the packet afterwards.
challenge.e.rt.egress: The longest-prefix-match lookup in the routing table for {{dst}} yields egress interface {{port}}.
challenge.e.rt.frag: With the DF bit set, fragmentation is not allowed. The router drops the packet ({{size}} bytes > MTU {{mtu}}) and reports “fragmentation needed” with the MTU (path MTU discovery).
challenge.e.rt.gateway: The host knows {{dst}} is not in its own subnet and sends the frame to its default gateway's MAC ({{mac}}). The IP address stays that of the final destination.
challenge.e.rt.nexthop.direct: The destination network is directly connected, so the next hop is the destination itself ({{via}}).
challenge.e.rt.nexthop.hop: The destination {{dst}} is behind another router; the next hop {{via}} from the routing table is the next router.
challenge.e.rt.noRoute: With no matching entry (not even a default route for {{dst}}) the router drops the packet and sends ICMP destination net unreachable to the sender.
challenge.e.rt.rewrite: A new frame is built at layer 2 (new source/destination MAC for the next segment). At layer 3 only the TTL (and checksum) changes; NAT would be the exception.
challenge.e.rt.ttl: Every router decrements the TTL by 1: {{inTtl}} becomes {{outTtl}}.
challenge.e.rt.ttlExpired: When the TTL reaches 0 the router drops the packet and reports ICMP time exceeded to {{src}}. This is exactly how traceroute works.
challenge.e.sw.action.drop: A port or VLAN rule forbids forwarding. A switch checks VLAN membership, the trunk allowed list and the spanning tree state before forwarding.
challenge.e.sw.action.filter: The destination sits on the port the frame arrived on. The switch filters the frame because it has already reached that segment.
challenge.e.sw.action.flood: The destination MAC is unknown or a broadcast/multicast. The switch sends the frame out all other ports of the VLAN ({{count}}), never back out the ingress port {{port}}.
challenge.e.sw.action.forward: Destination MAC {{dst}} is in the MAC table. A switch forwards known unicast frames only out the matching port ({{out}}).
challenge.e.sw.dropReason.noVlan: VLAN {{vlan}} is not created on the switch (show vlan brief).
challenge.e.sw.dropReason.outDown: The egress port is not in the forwarding state.
challenge.e.sw.dropReason.stpBlocked: Spanning tree blocks {{port}} in VLAN {{vlan}} to prevent loops.
challenge.e.sw.dropReason.taggedOnAccess: An access port expects untagged frames; {{port}} is not a trunk.
challenge.e.sw.dropReason.vlanNotAllowed: The trunk's allowed list ({{port}}) does not contain VLAN {{vlan}}.
challenge.e.sw.floodCount: Flooding goes out all active ports of the VLAN except {{port}}: {{count}} port(s) here.
challenge.e.sw.floodReason.bcast: ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff is the broadcast address: it is meant for every device in the VLAN, so it is flooded.
challenge.e.sw.floodReason.mcast: Without IGMP snooping, multicast MACs are flooded like broadcasts.
challenge.e.sw.floodReason.unknown: The destination {{dst}} has not been learned yet. Unknown unicast is flooded until the reply fills the MAC table.
challenge.e.sw.learn: A switch dynamically learns the source MAC {{src}} and ties it to the ingress port {{port}} – not the destination, and independent of ARP.
challenge.e.sw.port: The switch looks up {{dst}} in its MAC table and finds port {{out}}.
challenge.intro: What does the device do with this PDU? Pick the right action for each question – the answer is checked against the simulation's actual decision.
challenge.none: There are no questions for this event. Pick an event where a device makes a decision (switch, router, host).
challenge.o.aclLog: Only log it and forward it
challenge.o.aclReplyAdmin: ICMP destination unreachable, code 13 (communication administratively prohibited)
challenge.o.arpCache: Store {{ip}} → {{mac}} in the ARP cache and send the waiting packet
challenge.o.arpDropReply: Drop the reply – only routers need ARP replies
challenge.o.arpForward: Forward the reply to all other devices
challenge.o.arpNeeded: Yes – the MAC of {{via}} is not known yet, an ARP request follows
challenge.o.arpNotNeeded: No – the next hop's MAC is already in the ARP cache
challenge.o.arpReply: Answer {{sender}} with a unicast ARP reply (its own MAC)
challenge.o.arpReplyAny: Answer with its own MAC anyway
challenge.o.arpRoute: Route the request to the default gateway
challenge.o.closedAccept: Accept the packet and answer later
challenge.o.closedRst: A TCP segment with the RST flag
challenge.o.dropNoVlan: The VLAN does not exist on the switch
challenge.o.dropOutDown: The egress port is not forwarding
challenge.o.dropTagged: Tagged frame on an access port
challenge.o.dropVlanNotAllowed: The VLAN is not allowed on the trunk
challenge.o.echoForward: Forward the packet to the default gateway
challenge.o.fragFragment: Fragment it despite the DF bit
challenge.o.fragIcmp: Drop it and send ICMP “fragmentation needed” (MTU {{mtu}})
challenge.o.gwBcast: That is how the router asks all hosts to answer
challenge.o.gwError: A mistake – the destination MAC should be the destination host's
challenge.o.gwNormal: Normal: for destinations outside the subnet the host sends to its gateway's MAC
challenge.o.hubDrop: Inspect the frame and drop it if faulty
challenge.o.hubMac: Forward to the destination only, by MAC address
challenge.o.hubRepeat: Repeat the signal on all other ports
challenge.o.learnNone: Nothing – switches only learn from ARP packets
challenge.o.learnSrcOut: Source MAC {{src}} lives on the egress port
challenge.o.matchIdSeq: By the identifier and sequence number in the ICMP header
challenge.o.nicAccept: Accept and pass it to the IP layer
challenge.o.nicDiscard: Discard – the frame is not for this NIC
challenge.o.noRouteFlood: Send it out of all interfaces
challenge.o.noRouteQueue: Queue it until a route appears
challenge.o.noRouteUnreach: Drop it and send ICMP destination net unreachable to the sender
challenge.o.reasonBcast: The destination MAC is the broadcast address
challenge.o.reasonMcast: The destination MAC is a multicast address
challenge.o.reasonUnknown: The destination MAC is not in the MAC table (unknown unicast)
challenge.o.rewriteBoth: MAC and IP addresses are rewritten
challenge.o.rewriteIp: Only the IP addresses are rewritten, the MACs stay
challenge.o.rewriteMac: Source and destination MAC are rewritten, the IP addresses stay, the TTL drops by 1
challenge.o.rewriteNone: Nothing – the frame is passed on unchanged
challenge.o.rtDropAcl: Drop it because an ACL blocks it
challenge.o.rtDropNoRoute: Drop it because there is no route
challenge.o.rtDropTtl: Drop it because the TTL expired
challenge.o.swFilter: Drop because the destination is on the same port
challenge.o.swFlood: Flood out all other ports of the VLAN
challenge.o.swForward: Forward out exactly one port (entry in the MAC table)
challenge.o.ttlIcmp: Drop it and send ICMP time exceeded to {{src}}
challenge.o.ttlSilent: Drop it silently, without a message
challenge.q.acl.decision: ACL {{acl}} ({{dir}}) is applied on the interface. The packet {{src}} → {{dst}} is checked against it. What is the verdict?
challenge.q.acl.dir: In which direction was ACL {{acl}} applied?
challenge.q.acl.reply: What does the sender of the dropped packet get from a Cisco router?
challenge.q.gen.layer: Up to which layer does {{device}} process this PDU?
challenge.q.host.arpBcast: Which kind of layer 2 address was the ARP request sent to?
challenge.q.host.arpNotMine: An ARP request asks for {{ip}}, which is not this device's address. What does it do?
challenge.q.host.arpReply: The ARP reply says: {{ip}} is at {{mac}}. What does the device do with it?
challenge.q.host.arpReq: Someone asks “Who has {{ip}}?” (sender {{sender}}). The address belongs to this device. What does it do?
challenge.q.host.closedPort: A {{proto}} packet reaches port {{port}} where no service is listening. What does the host send back?
challenge.q.host.echoMatch: How does the sender match this echo reply to its echo request?
challenge.q.host.echoReq: An echo request from {{src}} arrives at the host's own address. What does the host do?
challenge.q.host.nic: The frame's destination MAC is {{dst}}, the NIC's MAC is {{mac}}. What does the NIC do?
challenge.q.host.notMine: The packet is addressed to {{dst}}, not to this host. What does the host do?
challenge.q.hub.action: A hub receives a signal. What does it do?
challenge.q.nat.in: The reply arrives at the inside global address {{global}}. To which address does the router forward it after reverse translation?
challenge.q.nat.out: The packet from inside host {{local}} leaves the network towards {{dst}}. Which source address does it carry afterwards?
challenge.q.rt.action: The router receives a packet {{src}} → {{dst}} with TTL {{ttl}}. What does it do?
challenge.q.rt.arp: Does the router first have to ARP for the MAC of the next hop {{via}} before sending?
challenge.q.rt.egress: Out of which interface does the router forward the packet to {{dst}}?
challenge.q.rt.frag: The packet is {{size}} bytes, the egress MTU is {{mtu}} and the DF bit is set. What does the router do?
challenge.q.rt.gateway: The frame's destination MAC is {{mac}} (the router's MAC) but the IP destination is {{dst}}. Why?
challenge.q.rt.nexthop: Which address is the next hop for {{dst}}?
challenge.q.rt.noRoute: The routing table has no route to {{dst}} (not even a default route). What does the router do?
challenge.q.rt.rewrite: What does the router change in the packet when forwarding (without NAT)?
challenge.q.rt.ttl: The packet arrives with TTL {{ttl}}. What TTL does it have after forwarding?
challenge.q.rt.ttlExpired: The packet {{src}} → {{dst}} arrives with TTL 1. What happens?
challenge.q.sw.action: The switch receives a frame with destination MAC {{dst}} in VLAN {{vlan}}. What does it do?
challenge.q.sw.dropReason: The switch drops the frame that arrived on {{port}}. Why?
challenge.q.sw.floodCount: On how many ports (VLAN {{vlan}}) does the switch send out the frame that arrived on {{port}}?
challenge.q.sw.floodReason: Why does the switch flood the frame (destination MAC {{dst}})?
challenge.q.sw.learn: What does the switch learn from this frame?
challenge.q.sw.port: Out of which port does the switch send the frame with destination MAC {{dst}}?
